options.metric: Annual sum of pedestrian injuries plus pedestrian deaths in police-reported Brooklyn motor vehicle crashes, calendar years 2013–2025
options.denominator: No separate denominator; annual sum across qualifying Brooklyn crash reports
options.reason: This captures the total recorded human burden and combines nonfatal and fatal pedestrian harm in one intuitive series.
options.answer: Only partly: reported pedestrian casualties totaled 3,671 in 2013 and 2,874 in 2025, reaching a low of 1,798 in 2020; these totals do not measure risk per walking trip.
options.interpretation: Only partly: the chart shows annual totals of reported pedestrian casualties in Brooklyn crashes, defined as the sum of pedestrians injured and killed per police-reported motor vehicle crash, grouped by crash year for complete calendar years 2013–2025; the total was 3,671 in 2013 and 2,874 in 2025, with a low of 1,798 in 2020. This is a defensible measure of recorded casualty burden, but it leaves unanswered whether an individual pedestrian trip became safer because there is no walking-exposure denominator. The data check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 NYC rows (30.9%) in 2013–2025 had missing, empty, or unknown borough and those rows were excluded; all 473,801 Brooklyn rows had both pedestrian fields present and nonnegative, so none were dropped for those fields. The partial 2026 records, observed only through June 11, were excluded.

options.metric: Annual sum of pedestrians killed in police-reported Brooklyn motor vehicle crashes, calendar years 2013–2025
options.denominator: No separate denominator; annual sum across qualifying Brooklyn crash reports
options.reason: Fatalities are a distinct and especially consequential outcome that should not be obscured by much more frequent nonfatal injuries.
options.answer: Only partly: reported pedestrian deaths were 30 in 2013 and 39 in 2025, with a peak of 46 in 2015 and a low of 17 in 2020; this is not a pedestrian-risk rate.
options.interpretation: Only partly: the chart shows annual counts of pedestrians killed in police-reported motor vehicle crashes assigned to Brooklyn, grouped by crash year for complete calendar years 2013–2025; the count was 30 in 2013 and 39 in 2025, with a peak of 46 in 2015. This isolates the most severe recorded pedestrian outcome, but it does not answer whether pedestrian risk per trip or distance walked changed, and crash-report totals are not adjusted for exposure. The data check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 NYC rows (30.9%) in 2013–2025 had missing, empty, or unknown borough and those rows were excluded; all 473,801 Brooklyn rows had a present, nonnegative pedestrian-death count, so none were dropped for that field. The partial 2026 records, observed only through June 11, were excluded.

options.metric: Annual percentage of qualifying Brooklyn crash reports recording at least one pedestrian injury or death, calendar years 2013–2025
options.denominator: Count of Brooklyn crash reports per year with both pedestrian injury and death counts present and nonnegative
options.reason: The share standardizes the pedestrian-casualty-report count by the number of Brooklyn crash reports, giving a report-level comparison alongside raw totals.
options.answer: Only partly: reports with a pedestrian injury or death were 7.44% of Brooklyn crash reports in 2013 and 11.38% in 2025, a report-level share rather than a measure of risk per walking trip.
options.interpretation: Only partly: the chart shows, for each complete calendar year from 2013 through 2025, the percentage of Brooklyn police-reported motor vehicle crashes with either at least one pedestrian injured or at least one pedestrian killed; the share was 7.44% in 2013 and 11.38% in 2025. This is a defensible report-level measure because its denominator is all Brooklyn crash reports with both pedestrian counts present and nonnegative, but it leaves pedestrian-trip risk unanswered. Between neighboring years 2019 and 2020, the denominator fell from 44,479 to 25,473 reports, a decrease of 19,006, the largest neighboring-year change in the check file; across those years, a rise or fall in the share can come from this denominator change rather than from the casualty outcome, so compare that interval with caution. The data check found 659,713 of 2,132,218 NYC rows (30.9%) in 2013–2025 had missing, empty, or unknown borough and those rows were excluded; all 473,801 Brooklyn rows had both pedestrian fields present and nonnegative, so they were retained, while partial 2026 (through June 11) was excluded.
